blocks.text: **"Take a sexual history from this 24-year-old woman."**
"Take a sexual history from this woman presenting with vaginal discharge."
"Assess this woman's risk of sexually transmitted infection."
"Take a history from a woman with deep dyspareunia."
"Take a sexual history from this patient with pelvic inflammatory disease."
"Take an appropriate sexual history from this adolescent."
The examiner is assessing **both information gathering and communication skills**.
❌ "How many sexual partners do you have?"
Instead, establish why you are asking.

"I'd like to ask you a few questions about your sexual health because they can sometimes help us understand symptoms such as pelvic pain, discharge or bleeding. I ask these questions routinely and everything we discuss is confidential. Is that okay?"
This gives you a comprehensive OSCE history.
"Do you have sex with men, women, or both?"
"Have you had any new sexual partners recently?"
"How many sexual partners have you had recently?"
Don't ask this in a judgmental tone.
This is an important part that candidates often omit.
"What types of sexual contact do you have?"
You need to establish the **type of sexual exposure** because different infections may be transmitted through different sexual practices and may require different sites of testing.
"Do you use condoms or other barrier protection?"
"How often would you say you use them?"
"Do you use condoms with all partners?"
"Have there been occasions when a condom has broken or slipped?"

subsections.subsection_title: 8. CONTRACEPTION IS NOT THE SAME AS STI PROTECTION

blocks.text: This is a common examiner point.
That protects against pregnancy but **does not protect against STIs**.
"What are you using to prevent pregnancy?"
"What are you using to protect against sexually transmitted infections?"
"Are you currently trying to avoid pregnancy, trying to become pregnant, or would a pregnancy be acceptable?"
This is an excellent question because it establishes the patient's **reproductive intention**.
"Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?"
"Have you ever been treated for pelvic inflammatory disease?"
**Tubal damage → infertility + increased ectopic pregnancy risk**
"Have you noticed any sores, ulcers or blisters around your genital area?"
"Have you noticed any lumps, growths or warts around your genital area?"
"Do you experience any pain during sexual intercourse?"
"Is the pain mainly at the entrance of the vagina or deeper inside?"
"Does it become worse around your period?"
because this combination should raise suspicion for **endometriosis**.
"Have you ever noticed bleeding after intercourse?"

If appropriate, make sure the patient is alone.
"I ask all my patients this because relationships and safety can affect health. Do you feel safe in your relationship?"
"Has anyone ever pressured or forced you to have sexual contact when you did not want to?"
"Has anyone ever physically hurt or threatened you?"

"I'd like to speak with you privately for part of the consultation, if that's okay."
Explain confidentiality and its limits in an age-appropriate way.
**"What would you tell the patient about confidentiality?"**

"I would explain that the information she provides is confidential and will normally only be shared with members of the healthcare team involved in her care. However, I would explain that confidentiality may have limits if there is a serious risk of harm to herself or someone else, or where safeguarding obligations require information to be shared."
❌ "Everything you tell me will remain completely secret."
This is an excellent addition to your history.
**"Are you currently trying to become pregnant, trying to avoid pregnancy, or are you unsure?"**
"Have you ever tried to become pregnant?"
Certain conditions and medications affect sexual health.

blocks.text: "This is a 24-year-old sexually active woman presenting with a five-day history of abnormal vaginal discharge and dysuria. She has recently started a sexual relationship with a new partner and reports inconsistent condom use. She has no previous history of diagnosed STIs but reports mild lower abdominal discomfort and deep dyspareunia."
"My main considerations would include cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease, and I would assess her clinically and arrange appropriate STI testing."

"This is a 31-year-old woman with a two-year history of deep dyspareunia associated with severe dysmenorrhoea and cyclical pelvic pain. She has been trying to conceive for 18 months without success. She has no significant STI history."

"This is a 26-year-old woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge and deep dyspareunia. She has a recent new sexual partner and inconsistent condom use. She reports fever but no vomiting or urinary symptoms."

"This is a 35-year-old woman presenting with recurrent postcoital bleeding over three months. She also reports intermittent vaginal discharge but no significant pelvic pain. I would clarify her cervical screening history, STI risk and associated symptoms and would require appropriate cervical and pelvic assessment."

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What is the 5 Ps framework?

blocks.text: **Partners, Practices, Protection from STIs, Past history of STIs and Prevention of pregnancy.**

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Why ask about sexual practices?

blocks.text: Because different sexual practices can expose different anatomical sites to infection and therefore influence the appropriate examination and testing.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. Why distinguish contraception from STI protection?

blocks.text: Because most contraceptive methods prevent pregnancy but do not protect against STIs. Condoms provide barrier protection against many STIs as well as contraception.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What are the major risk factors for PID?

blocks.text: Previous STI/PID, new or multiple sexual partners, inconsistent condom use and other circumstances associated with increased STI exposure.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What are complications of PID?

blocks.text: **Infertility, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy and tubo-ovarian abscess.**

**I** — Infertility
**C** — Chronic pelvic pain
**E** — Ectopic pregnancy
**A** — Abscess

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What is the significance of deep dyspareunia?

blocks.text: It may indicate pelvic pathology such as endometriosis, PID, adnexal disease or pelvic adhesions.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What is the most important thing to establish when asking about sexual assault?

blocks.text: **Whether the sexual activity was consensual and whether the patient is currently safe.**
Especially in adolescent and safeguarding stations.
"How many men have you slept with?"
"Have you had any other sexual partners recently?"
If an STI is diagnosed, ask whether partners have been assessed and treated.
**Trying to conceive vs avoid pregnancy vs ambivalent.**

"Are you currently sexually active? What types of sexual contact do you have? Do you have a new or multiple partners? Do you use condoms, and how consistently? Have you ever had an STI or been treated for PID? Are you currently using contraception? Are you trying to become pregnant or avoid pregnancy? Have you experienced vaginal discharge, genital ulcers, dysuria, pelvic pain, dyspareunia or postcoital bleeding? Do you feel safe in your relationship, and has anyone ever pressured or forced you to have sexual contact?"
That is a **very strong rapid sexual-history framework**.
